newsitem.title: UK: Analysts see lower world sugar prices, more stocks.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see lower world sugar prices, more stocks.

text.p: World sugar prices should succumb to the weight of a hefty surplus in 1996/97, spurred by rising stocks that are unlikely to be totally absorbed by higher demand, analysts said on Friday.
World sugar markets should see a second consecutive year of surplus, although the excess will be sharply reduced.

Estimates of the exact amounts vary according to the time period used, but the sugar trade's most respected analysts now seem to agree that prices are set to fall. Trade house E D & F Man recently forecast production at 123.54 million tonnes raw value in 1996/97, slightly higher than the previous year. But with consumption forecast to rise by only one million tonnes to 119.91 million, the global surplus should increase by two million tonnes to 3.62 million.

The latest estimate, released by the International Sugar Organization (ISO) on Friday, said prices would sink to 10 cents per pound from current levels of around 10.80 cents. "It'll take some time but we think that the downward pressure will continue," said Tony Hannah, analyst at the ISO.
"Consumption (growth) is quite stable if you look at the year-on-year increase, it's just that production has levelled off and consumption is catching up a bit," he said.
Man said prices would be depressed by the possibility of raw sugar exports from key producer India and the release of white sugar exports from Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
India, where most of the world 1996/97 surplus is trapped, will be a determining factor in the equation as it is sitting on stocks representing 60 percent of annual consumption.
It could export as much as 200,000 tonnes of raws as millers search for additional export markets, Man said.
But analysts said Indian ports would be hard pressed to manage such a huge quantity at one go, so the market would not be flooded with a rush of sugar.
India's internal sugar price would also suffer, which might be politically undesirable, they added.

"They don't really want to kill whatever income stream they do have," said Chris Pack, senior analyst at Czarnikow Sugar. "It might win them a few consumer votes but there are an awful lot of Indian farmers and factory workers in the sugar industry."

World sugar imports are set to fall as demand ebbs from key buyers China and Russia, and analysts said the expected decline in EU production did not necessarily signal lower exports due to sugar carried over outside the trading bloc's growing quota.

The EU, the world's largest exporter of sugar to the free market, has a highly regulated policy which subsidises farmers and holds internal prices sufficiently high to give adequate returns for growing beet even in less efficient areas.
